newsitem.title: HONG KONG: YEAREND-Hong Kong, Asian stocks seen strong in '97.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-Hong Kong, Asian stocks seen strong in '97.

text.p: Asia will retake ground lost to other emerging market regions in 1997 following a year in which Russia, Eastern Europe and Latin America stole the limelight, Asian fund managers told Reuters.
"We expect some of these economies which have been depressed by the export slowdown should look more favourable next year," said Marcel Souza, senior economist at LGT Asset Management.
Stocks in Hong Kong will continue to out-perform in 1997 after a 30-percent rise this year on renewed optimism about the British colony's future after its return to China next July 1.
Many Asian fund managers put the Hang Seng index at 15,000 by July 1997, with further gains possible on the back of a rebounding Chinese economy.

Fund managers said heavily overweighted positions in Hong Kong stocks, some approaching 50 percent of Far East Asian ex-Japan portfolios, would remain unchanged and could even increase early next year.

In Japan, low interest rates, financial deregulation and gradual improvements in a weak economy are expected to push the Nikkei 225 index up to about 25,000 by the end of 1997 against the 1996 high of 22,750, fund managers said.

"The index can rise as high as 26,000 though it's hard to predict at what level it would be settled. I think you can take a bullish stance for next year," said Soichi Okuda, senior economist with Tokyo Securities Co Ltd.
While economic uncertainty could weigh on smaller Asian markets at first, improving economic fundamentals will draw new money into the region later in the year, fund managers said.

Driving the enthusiasm are early signs of an export turnaround in Asia following this year's sorry showing, along with expectations that higher U.S. interest rates will depress U.S. stocks and send money flying to the Far East.
"The big trick is when do people reduce (Hong Kong) and go into other markets," said Graham Muirhead, director at HSBC Asset Management in Hong Kong.
Other fund managers said regional market strength will prompt a new wave of funds into the entire region, providing a second, third or even fourth wind for the Hang Seng index.

"I think you'll find these other econmies will come around and Asia will attract more money. That won't take from Hong Kong, it'll be new money," said Christopher Day, joint managing director at Thornton Management (Asia) Ltd.
Day dismissed concerns about a mid-December market correction which wiped 269 points off the Hang Seng index on Friday, closing on Friday at 12,784.
"It will correct down below 13,000 and then get back on track to 14,000 and up to 16,000," he said.
Greater confidence in a smooth transition to Chinese rule prompted a re-rating of Hong Kong stocks in 1996 as investors started to remove a long-held political discount.
Credit easing and a buoyant Chinese economy will support the market through the coming year, with many fund managers reporting aggressive buying of red chips to gain access to the China growth story.

Malaysian stocks chased Hong Kong higher throughout 1996 and more strength is seen on the back of a narrowing current account deficit, expectations of easing interest rates and evidence of steady economic growth and consumer confidence.
Singapore, most exposed to a turnaround in demand for electronics from the United Sates, will recover this year but sluggish consumer spending could delay significant strength.
Taiwan rose on its inclusion in Morgan Stanley's indices for the first time, with further gains forecast on an improving economy and access to the China market.
The Philippines reported the best earnings growth in the region, with more to follow next year, while Indonesia was a steady performer.

"In Indonesia, earnings growth is strong, inflation is coming down, rates are structurally too high and will continue to come down, but stock valuations are attractive on earnings forecasts," said Muirhead.
Thailand and South Korea were the two greatest disappointments in of 1996 and the outlook remains cautious for both markets.
Although South Korean stocks might gain on improved demand for its electronics exports, high interest rates will cotninue to depress the market.
In Thailand, few were prepared to forecast recovery at this point or target a turnaround time next year.
